meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This is also true of the activities of the judiciary in the state courts.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It may be felt appropriate to provide a definition clarifying which of these bodies are expressly excluded from the scope of the VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The precise terms used need to be adapted to make sense in the context of the organization of government of the particular state.49 B.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Excluding Persons with Low Levels of Business Activity Most states require only some of the many persons active in business within the state to be taxable persons.50

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This is normally achieved by setting a minimum level or threshold of business activity and requiring only those persons with levels of activity above the minimum to be taxable persons.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Those with levels of activity below that level are not required to be taxable 47 OECD Model Tax Convention, supra note 40, art.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The key test for registration is normally whether a taxable person makes supplies of the required level within the state.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For that purpose, it does not matter in what form the supplier is present in the state—although in practice it may prove difficult to identify the person who ought to register by reason of a single transaction.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Residence is, however, relevant to some supplies of services and for certain procedural purposes (e.g., nonresidents being required to appoint a resident tax representative).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: One approach that accepts this problem is that of the United Kingdom in providing that "a supply of services shall be treated as made . . .

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: in the United Kingdom if the supplier belongs in the United Kingdom . . . "

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A supplier of services is treated as "belonging," if there is a business establishment in the country.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Either a branch or an agency is treated as a business establishment.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: "Branch or agency" is the phrase used in U.K. income tax law instead of "permanent establishment."

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The phrase used in the underlying EU law is "fixed establishment."

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This is the same term as that used in the French version of the OECD Model Double Tax Convention for "permanent establishment."

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: 259, and the French version of the Swiss law, OTVA art.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It must also be noted that the concept of permanent establishment is not without its own problems.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, if a business has a permanent establishment within the jurisdiction, is that establishment deemed to supply all supplies made to the jurisdiction by the company, even though they are not made through the permanent establishment?

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It may be so treated under the "force of attraction" principle, cf.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: 5, which is, however, rejected by many treaties for income tax purposes.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For the position relating to the diplomatic and consular functions of the state, see infra sec. IV(K).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: 50 Some states, however, require all legal persons to be registered and have a minimum limit for individuals only.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: States may also exclude certain kinds of activity (e.g., excluding retailers but taxing wholesalers).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This is usually considered problematic and contrary to the spirit of the VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 15 - persons, although they are often given the right to voluntarily choose to be taxable persons.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The usual measure of business activity is the total turnover of taxable goods and services supplied by the person over a set period.51for a set period, the result may be seen to be unfair.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The total to be taken into account for the threshold is the total taxable supplies of that person.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This means the total of all supplies made by that person that are treated as taxable supplies within the definition of the law.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The total does not include supplies exempted from VAT or outside the scope of VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This means that a person conducting a business that is largely exempt is outside the scope of the registration provisions if the taxable activities reach a total less than the threshold, although the total economic activity of the business is high.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The precise level of threshold varies widely from one state to another and, within a state, varies from one time to another.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Limits vary partly as a reflection of the economic structure of a state.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Some states have a comparatively greater number of marginal small businesses involving one person or one family than other states.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Even taking account of the differences, in many states self-employed individuals or single families engaged, for example, in subsistence farming or small market trading will contribute little to the collection of VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It is also administratively difficult—and therefore expensive—to collect tax from such people.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In addition, the exclusion of smaller traders from VAT through the use of a threshold limit is particularly useful at the introduction of the tax, when there are limits on available administrative resources and taxpayer knowledge of the tax is at a minimum.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The law may be drafted to allow the authorities to alter the amount set from time to time, both to ensure that the tax is working properly and, in any event, to ensure that inflation does not have too significant an effect on the practical level of the threshold.52as the minimum monthly or annual wage.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The threshold then adjusts automatically with that factor.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This discussion assumes that a law has only one registration limit.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Some states have more than one limit, for example, a lower limit by reference to the supplies of services or of certain kinds of services, and another, higher limit for the supply of goods.53 This allows the state 51

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The threshold will need to be defined with some care.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: There are two bases for definition: actual turnover of taxable supplies over a defined period and estimated turnover over a defined period.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The test may be based on past periods (when actual turnover can be used), future periods (when estimates must be used), or a period such as the current calendar year, which is both past and future.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: An estimate might be based on the amount that it is reasonable to assume or, alternatively, likely that the business will exceed.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The advantage of including estimates is that this allows registration to be made mandatory before the threshold is reached.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: However, there will be situations where the estimate proves to be too high, and registration is forced in a case where it was not objectively required.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In such a case, if other provisions force a registration to remain 52 This provision is extremely sensitive in economies with high inflation.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In some states that have severe problems with inflation, but that may not have a well-developed index of consumer prices, the practice has been adopted of linking the threshold not to a set sum of money but to an indexed factor, such 53 This happens in Ireland, where the higher limit applies to traders with at least 90 percent of their taxable turnover deriving from the sale of goods, with the lower threshold (about half the level of the higher threshold) applying to all other taxable persons.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 16 - authorities to impose limits that reflect the different proportions of value added involved in providing goods and providing services, although it can do so only by adding another level of complexity.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A provision setting more than one threshold will also need to provide a definition of the kinds of supply that count toward the lower level rather than the higher level and to provide for those who make both kinds of supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It should be emphasized that the threshold limit applies to all supplies made by one person or by that person's agent for the person.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It is possible for a person who is potentially a taxable person to avoid that result by transferring some of the person's activities to another person (who might be under common ownership with the person transferring).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: States concerned by such practices may adopt provisions requiring that the total of activities in such situations be added together and be deemed to be the activities of one taxpayer.54 It must also be clear that, apart from aggregation rules, the threshold applies separately to each taxable person.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, if A and B, both being active in business independently, also form a partnership, then the threshold applies separately to the taxable turnover of A, of B, and of the partnership.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: C. A VAT Register To administer the VAT, it is standard practice to establish a formal state register of those who are registered persons.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: There must then be a requirement that any person who is, or should be, a taxable person take the necessary action to seek to be registered for the VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The law or regulations need to confirm the register and give it official status.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Penalties will also be needed to ensure that all those required to do so apply to be registered.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Recognizing this requirement, laws sometimes refer to taxable persons as "registered persons" or "persons required to register.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: D. VAT Numbers States sometimes decide to adopt and adapt an existing register, such as the register for companies or a general register of taxpayers, to act as the VAT register.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: That is for a state to decide, but the register must be capable of generating a unique VAT number for each taxable 54 An example of this kind of antiavoidance provision is found in the United Kingdom.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This was strengthened considerably by the U.K. Finance Act 1996, sched.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The tax authorities can treat a series of separate companies as carrying on one trade so as to require them or one of them to register on behalf of the "group."

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The Japanese law has a "substantial attribution" rule based on similar rules for the direct taxes under which those who substantially enjoy consideration for transfers are regarded as the entities making the transfers.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A taxable person manipulating levels of transfer will be within the scope of this provision.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 17 - person,56 as well as providing the tax authorities with an up-to-date list of those, and only those, who are taxable persons.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For reasons of good administration, states with more limited administrative resources find it increasingly attractive that the VAT number be the same as the taxpayer identification number used for income and other taxes.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The practice must meet the need to provide all those registered for VAT, whether or not they are income tax payers, with a unique number at the time they are registered for VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The VAT number is used by the tax authorities and by taxable persons themselves to ensure the proper operation of an invoice-based VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Every invoice is important to the tax authorities wishing to collect the VAT recorded on it and also to any taxable person paying the VAT recorded on the invoice to ensure deduction of the input tax on the invoice.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For this reason, it is necessary to be able to identify the taxable person charging the VAT on the invoice.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The law should provide that a taxable person is under a duty to put his, her, or its VAT number on the invoice, so that this can be achieved.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Once a taxable person has been issued a VAT registration number or has had the registration confirmed under a given number, the law should require the person to use that number on all official communications.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, the number should be indicated on all communications with the tax authorities and perhaps other documents, such as official orders or official stationery.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: E. Voluntary Registration States often allow those who are not required to be registered (because their activities are below the level of the threshold) to register voluntarily.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This may be appropriate for many organizations that intend to have a large turnover, but have not yet reached it; incur large expenditure in one year, expecting the income in the next year; or are carrying out business activities at a level that does not reach the registration limit, but that do not wish this information to be known by customers (e.g., younger self-employed providers of services).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Voluntary registration also allows those operating just below the threshold level to avoid any competitive disadvantage compared with other operators who are required to be registered.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: There is sometimes a danger to the integrity of a tax system in allowing uncontrolled voluntary registration.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: First, this may allow those who are not in reality engaged in business to register with a view to claiming rebates of input tax when they have no real intention of paying much output tax.57 Such persons should not be entitled to register unless they are genuinely 56 The precise nature of the number used, and its status as a unique registration number for VAT purposes, is particularly important where the registration number is used in international transactions.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Best practice will require both that the number identify the taxable person by reference to the state issuing the number and that the number contain a check digit so that routine checks can be made against mistakes and deliberate wrong use of numbers.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: International identification is provided within the EU by a standard international prefix.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The check digit requires that the number be issued or monitored using standard mathematical methods.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: 57Some of the states adopting a VAT in recent years have experienced problems with this kind of fraud.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 18 - involved in business, but both practical and legal safeguards are needed to ensure that the tax authorities can control this situation.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Failure to control it may result in significant revenue loss.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It may be deterred to some extent by placing a minimum period on voluntary registration, as noted below.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A second reason for limiting voluntary registration is that the right to register voluntarily may have the effect of making many more persons "taxable persons" than is administratively appropriate for the state, particularly when a VAT is first introduced and the state has chosen to set a high threshold level.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Provided that the tax authorities can ensure that the integrity of the VAT is safeguarded, economic neutrality will be achieved only if voluntary registration is allowed.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A compromise adopted by some states introducing a VAT is to set a minimum activity level for compulsory registration and a lower minimum level for voluntary registration.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Where these rules operate, a person can register voluntarily only if the lower minimum is met.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This excludes those persons with no real economic activity or whose businesses have not yet started.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: At the same time, it allows some voluntary registration to control distortions between those just above and those just below the compulsory threshold.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: F. Exporters and Persons Engaged in International Activities Most states provide that there is no VAT on exports.58See supra sec. I(D).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: To avoid exporters paying VAT, provision is made for them to claim back any input tax they have paid in making the exports (see below).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Therefore, exporters and those in a similar position must be brought onto the register.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If they are not on the register, they will not be entitled to claim rebates of input tax, and their activities will be affected.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: An exporter may not have a level of activity great enough to be above the minimum level requiring registration.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Any provision in the law having the effect of excluding voluntary registration must therefore be accompanied by another provision ensuring that exporters are allowed to register regardless of their level of activity.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: G. Effect of Nonregistration A person who is required to register for the VAT is a "taxable person" who is subject to the duty to impose and collect VAT on all supplies whether or not the person is registered.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It is important that the law make this clear and not exclude a person from the scope of the law just because of a failure (deliberate or otherwise) on the part of the person to apply for registration.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It will also be appropriate to impose penalties on those who should have applied for registration but have failed to do so, as well as to ensure that full powers exist to collect VAT from those persons in respect of all supplies that have taken place (or are assumed or estimated to have taken place) when the person was not registered but should have been registered.59 However, such a person is 58

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This follows from adoption of the destination basis of taxation.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The amount collected is typically reduced by input tax credits supported by invoices.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 19 - not entitled to issue VAT invoices.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Hence, the person's customers cannot claim input tax credits in respect of supplies from such a person.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The converse to this position should also be made clear in the law.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A person who is not registered for VAT and is not required to be registered is outside the scope of the law.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A person outside the scope of the law has no right to claim a rebate for any input tax paid.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The person also has no right to impose VAT, or anything purporting to be VAT, on supplies made by the person.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: To ensure that persons do not abuse this position, two safeguards may be put in place.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: First, a person who collects or tries to collect VAT while not empowered to do so is made liable to criminal penalties.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Second, the VAT law provides powers to collect the sums of money from such a person although the sums are strictly not VAT.60

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A variant on the second provision is to ensure that the overpaid VAT is repaid to the person overpaying.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: H. Cancellation of Registration The law should provide for three situations where VAT registration should be canceled.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The first case is where a person has been registered for VAT properly, but where the registration is no longer appropriate.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This will occur where a person was required to register because the person's business activities exceeded the threshold but where, subsequently, the person's level of business activities has declined to below the threshold.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If the person is continuing in business, then, if the person so wishes, a voluntary registration may be maintained.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: However, the person should have the right to deregister.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Mechanisms are needed to allow a person to remove the person's name from the register when this occurs.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The second case is where the person has ceased to carry on business activities (or has ceased to qualify for some reason for voluntary registration).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If so, the person's name should be removed from the register whether or not the person applies for deregistration.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Subject to safeguards for the integrity of the VAT collection process, deregistration should take place when the person ceases to be entitled to register or no longer wishes to be registered.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The third case is where the person has been registered by mistake or by misrepresentation on the part of the person.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In these cases, it will usually be appropriate to provide that the person is removed from the register retrospectively to the moment of registration.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In other words, the registering authorities can take action so that the person registered wrongly can be treated as if the registration had never occurred.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The charging provisions of the law should deal with VAT liability that arises by reason of a person ceasing to be registered.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In addition, the powers of the tax authorities should remain in place notwithstanding the deregistration to deal with such charges.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The New Zealand law provides the Commissioner of Taxes with the power to collect the tax in these circumstances by an assessment if "[a]ny person, not being a registered person, supplies goods and services and represents that tax is charged on that supply . . ."

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 20 - Safeguards are needed to deal with those who have been registered, but should not have been registered, and for those who appear to be registering properly, but who use registration to obtain large refunds of input tax without later paying in any corresponding output tax.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In part, these safeguards may be linked to the grant of refunds for input tax.61 Some states add further safeguards, for example, preventing a person who has registered voluntarily from deregistering within a set time (perhaps one or two years) of first registering.62 J. Continuing a Registration Despite a Change in the Taxable Person Situations will arise where a person ceases carrying on a business unavoidably.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, the death, incapacity, or insolvency of an individual or the winding up of a company may mean that the person registered as running a business is no longer running it.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The business will usually continue at least for a time to be run by some other person.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, the trustee in bankruptcy or a receiver for a debtor may run the business in the owner's place, and the personal representatives of a deceased person will often run the business until it can be transferred to some other person.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In these cases, states often make provision to treat the registration as continuing notwithstanding the change in identity of the taxable person.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Rules might deal similarly with changes in membership of a partnership where the partnership continues to run the business without a break.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: These provisions should be linked with other provisions preventing a transfer of title in cases of continuing registration from constituting a supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The rules can be more liberal than the reorganization provisions of the income tax.63 III.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Supplies of Goods and Services A. Transactions within the Scope of the Law A broad-based VAT is designed to bring within its charge every kind of economic transaction, subject to limited exceptions.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This is normally achieved by drafting a very broad provision imposing VAT on an extremely wide range of business transactions and then removing by specific exception any transaction that is not to be liable.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Transactions are usually stated to be within the scope of VAT if they are "supplies of goods or services."

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: These terms are given extremely wide meanings that go significantly beyond the usual meanings of "supplies," "goods," and "services" in most languages.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The aim is to bring within the charge all economic activity.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In particular, the terms need to cover transactions 61

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: 9. 63I f a reorganization were to be considered a taxable supply, the successor entity would obtain an input tax credit in the same amount.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The logic of VAT does not require tax to be imposed in such a situation, as long as the successor continues to be a taxable person.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 21 - dealing with land or other immovable property and with intellectual property rights.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Therefore, the terms should not be limited to the meanings of those terms, for example, in consumer law.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For reasons of linguistic simplicity, all the relevant transactions are termed "supplies" in most English VAT texts.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: However, there is no one concept of "supply" in many languages.64 A more formal presentation of the scope of a VAT law might refer to (a) transactions involving the transfer of the legal rights to goods, and (b) other transactions within the scope of VAT but not involving such a transfer.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In actual drafting, one can employ less clumsy expressions than this, as long as the underlying intent is not lost.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The discussion will deal with the formal classification.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Besides identifying what transactions are within the scope of the VAT, rules are required to determine where transactions occur, when they occur, and who for the purposes of VAT is carrying out, or treated as carrying out, the transactions.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: B. Supplies of Goods VAT laws usually contain a definition of a "supply of goods" or "goods."

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It is felt, in the light of the formal presentation above, that the better practice is to offer a definition of a "supply of goods."

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Again, the definition needs to avoid being too closely related to any definition of a similar concept in the commercial or consumer law of the state.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This is because the scope of the VAT rule will usually be wider than the scope of the commercial law.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Other rules, such as timing, may also be different.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Nonetheless, those defining a "supply of goods" in the VAT context might well gain from reviewing the other definitions within the state of those terms.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A possible definition65 of a "supply of goods" is a transfer of the right to dispose of tangible movable property or of immovable property other than land.66of services, and leasing is 64 See supra sec. I(B).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The EC Sixth VAT Directive defines "supply of goods" as "the transfer of the right to dispose of tangible property as owner."

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This is an English rendering of the French "le transfert du pouvoir de disposer d'un bien meuble corporel comme un propriétaire," FRA CGI art.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: 256, and does not fully convey the civil code technicalities of the French version.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The Swiss-French version is "le pouvoir de disposer économiquement d'un bien en son propre nom."

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The U.K. law does not define "supply" (beyond saying that it includes all forms of supply, GBR VAT § 5(2)(a), a formula also adopted by the New Zealand law, NZL GST § 5(1)), or "goods" (defined in New Zealand, NZL GST § 2(1)) or "supply of goods."

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The Basic World Tax Code defines supply as "the act of providing a good or service . . ."

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Some definitions also expressly exclude "money" from the definition.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, the New Zealand definition states that "goods" includes "all kinds of personal or real property; but does not include choses in action or money."

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: (Chose in action means a right to bring a lawsuit or to recover a sum of money.)

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This is the widest definition possible in the context of the present form of law.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Other forms of property such as intellectual property are therefore not goods.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This is, however, an approach made within the context of the common law.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Other systems of law do not draw the same distinctions between tangible and intangible property.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, under the Japanese consumption tax law, the leasing of assets (goods) is treated in the same way as sales of assets and separately from the provision Tax Law Design and Drafting (volume 1; International Monetary Fund: 1996; Victor Thuronyi, ed.)

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 22 - defined to include transfers of intangible property in assets.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The consequence of this form of definition, coupled with a broad definition of services (see sec.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: D below), is that the transfer of intangible property will be considered a service.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The problem with a general definition of this concept is that there are fundamental differences in approach to the sales of goods in different legal systems, including differences within the European Union between common law states and civil law states.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The definition offered here is a compromise between the common law and civil law approaches to property.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The definition in a state may need to be aligned more closely with the property laws of that state.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, the common law approach identifies property as tangible (items that can be held or touched—usually referred to as goods or products in commercial laws) and intangible (property that cannot be touched, such as legal rights).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It also distinguishes between "personal property" (including tangible property that can be owned by individual persons, such as goods) and "real property" (this includes only legal rights of ownership to land and things attached to or inseparable from land).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In countries with a civil law tradition, a distinction is drawn between movable property and immovable property on a differing basis (e.g., a building can be treated as separate from the land on which the building stands, and the categories of immovable property may be related more to the physical ability to move the property than to the underlying legal rights).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: VAT laws may not precisely follow either of these approaches.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The objective of the VAT rule is to impose tax on the economic substance of what is occurring (and for which a person receives payment) rather than on its precise legal form.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A "supply of goods" is not constituted merely by a transfer of possession, which is a transfer of the use of goods, not of the goods themselves.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A transfer of the use of goods is a supply of services.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: What constitutes the right to dispose of property depends on the laws of each state.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The definition set out above avoids reference to a sale of the goods or the rights of ownership.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The intention is to avoid complexities of the commercial laws of a state, such as reservations of title, that may prevent ownership from transferring but that do not prevent all the physical attributes and economic value of ownership from being transferred.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Equally, a transaction that has all the attributes of a sale but later turns out to be avoidable for legal reasons does not thereby cease to be a supply, although there may later be a supply back again if the goods are transferred back.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If a transfer of possession (a supply of a service) is followed by a transfer of the title, or rights of ownership, the supply of goods is the supply of those rights and reflects the residual value after taking into account the value of the services already supplied.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: No separate definition of "goods" is needed save the explanation in the above definition or its equivalent.67

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The intention is to include in the category of "goods" all those forms of 67 For alternative approaches, see supra notes 65 and 66; see also Hussey & Lubick, supra note 13, § 212(a), (c) (defining "goods" as well as "supply").

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For a lengthy definition of "supply," see NZL GST § 5.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 23 - tangible property that are to be within the scope of the tax.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Land is often excluded from the definition of goods deliberately for reasons discussed below.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This will depend in part on how money is viewed in the property laws of a state (particularly, whether money is regarded as tangible or intangible).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In reality, whether or not money is excluded here, all forms of VAT exclude a charge to VAT on transfers of money (or, properly, the use of money) by exemption.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Any exclusion of property or transactions from the definition of "supply of goods" will bring it within the definition of "supply of services" set out below, thereby requiring the exclusion to be set forth again.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Many laws also extend the definition of supplies of goods to cover supplies of energy and other kinds of supply that are similar to goods.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, a supply of electricity is not generally treated under civil or commercial law as a supply of goods, nor is a supply of heat, refrigeration, or air conditioning.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: However, it is usually regarded as convenient to treat them as supplies of goods to apply the timing and location rules that relate to goods.68 C. Land

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The reference to "immovable property other than land" is designed to take account of the fact that some states have wider definitions of immovable property than other states.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Whatever the scope of the definitions within a state, a sale of land should be excluded from the scope of a supply of goods.69 "Land" in this context means the rights of a person as the owner to legal title and exclusive possession and control over any part of the surface or subsoil of the territory of the state.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The emphasis is on the legal title, not on the actual soil.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This may or may not automatically include legal title and possession of any buildings, structures, or equipment fixed to the surface or in the subsoil.70

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The reference to legal title is based on the assumption that the law of the state provides for the sale of the whole legal interest in land.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In a number of states, only limited sales of interests in land can occur and to that extent the comments are not relevant.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

meta.creator: Unknown

meta.creator: Unknown

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It also applies in states, such as those of the former Soviet Union, where land cannot be sold, but a building on the land can be sold.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 25 - A "supply of services" is often defined as any supply within the scope of VAT that is not a supply of goods or a supply of land.76 This definition, when read with the definition of "supply of goods" means that any supply is within the scope of the charge to VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If that is so, it may be asked why there is any need to distinguish between "goods" and "services."

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The answer is that the rules locating a supply of services are different from those for a supply of goods, as are the rules determining when such supplies occur.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Further, where VAT is charged at more than one rate, the precise identity of the supply may be critical.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Also, the self-supply rules explained below apply to goods but not to services.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Finally, a supply of goods across the frontier of a state is an import or export of those goods and is subject to the customs regime of the state.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The latter point serves to emphasize that, in cases of doubt, it may be useful to consider the scope of the customs law of the state in considering whether or not something is a "good."

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It is therefore not possible77 to have a supply that is not either a supply of goods or a supply of services, except for supplies of land or money.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: From this, it is clear that "services" has an extended meaning.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It covers the use of all forms of property and also transfers of the right to dispose of intangible property.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It also covers negative events, such as refraining from activity or undertaking by covenant or agreement not to do something.78 Indeed, "services" are supplied whenever value is added because of a transaction that falls within the scope of VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A transaction will fall within the scope of VAT under the normal rules if the transaction is a business transaction, if the person making the supply is a taxable person, and if some other person makes a payment for the supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: VAT laws rarely offer a useful separate definition of "supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A supply will occur whenever there is some transaction or event involving a taxable person whereby the taxable person receives payment (or consideration) for the effects of that transaction or event.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In other words, the concept of value added is reflected by this broad definition.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Any narrower definition, and any attempt to place limits on the meaning of "supply" or of "services," would exclude economic activities from the scope of VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: 76 Est considérée comme prestation de services toute prestation qui ne constitue pas la livraison d'un bien."

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In the European Union, "supply of services shall mean any transaction which does not constitute a supply of goods."

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Where goods are defined as excluding money, it is appropriate to provide that "services means anything which is not goods or money."

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The Japanese law has no equivalent and relies instead on a comprehensive list of kinds of service.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, the U.K. law provides that the transfer of an ongoing business is a supply, but of neither goods nor services.
