text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 26 - Interpretation and application of this provision should reflect this broad policy approach because it ensures not only efficiency in collecting the tax but also fairness between one taxable person and another.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It is only if all economic activities that add similar value are taxed similarly that a fair and easily administrable tax can exist.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Comment has already been made about the exclusion of land and money from the definition of supply of goods.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If the above definitional structure for supply of services is used, it is necessary to repeat those exclusions in the definition of supply of services.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The law should provide that the service undertaken by an employee for the employer of that employee does not form a supply made by that employee.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Two ways of doing this are to expressly say so or to ensure that an employee can never be a taxable person, by providing that a person is a taxable person in respect only of supplies made by that person independently.80

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The rule also covers all those holding office, such as company directors and all government officers and employees.81 F. Supplies by Agents Where a supplier supplies goods or services through an agent to another person, the supply is made not by the agent but by the supplier.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Whether in a particular case an intermediary is an agent will depend on the precise legal nature of the contract between the persons involved.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The employee's service, if supplied directly or indirectly to a third person, is a supply by the employer.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This rule covers all supplies from employees, including the case where an employee works directly for some third person, if the third person contracts with, and pays, the employer.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If the employee is seconded to the third person and is paid directly by that third person, then the true relationship may be that the employee is now employed by the third person.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If the third person makes no payment to the employer, then the payment to the employee will probably not constitute consideration between the employer and the third person, so that there is nothing on which VAT is to be paid.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: An agent is normally entitled to a fee or commission for services rendered to a supplier, and VAT is charged on those services (unless they are exempt).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Where an agent is used, it is therefore for the supplier, not the agent, to charge VAT and to pay it to the budget.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Special powers may be considered necessary to enforce payment of VAT by an agent where the agent, rather than the supplier, has the money to make payment and the supplier has not paid.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: 80 See the definition of taxable person in EC Sixth VAT Directive, supra note 3, art. 4(1), on which this text is based.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The reference is to "independent workers" rather than to "dependent workers."

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: 81 See also the discussion on employment status in connection with social security, infra ch. 11, and income tax, vol. 2, ch. 14.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 27 - One special case is that of a sale by auction, or other forms of sale where the agent does not reveal that there is an agency or declines to reveal the identity of the person for whom the agent is acting.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Therefore, it may not even be clear whether the supplier is or is not a taxable person.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In such cases, it is necessary to treat the agent as a principal for the purposes of charging VAT to customers and to include rules requiring that this be the case, whatever the underlying legal relationships.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The effect of this is to require the agent (if a taxable person) to issue invoices to the customer and for the principal (if a taxable person) to issue invoices to the agent for the items sold.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In practice, it is often difficult to identify the nature of a supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Often what is supplied is a mixture of different things and often of both goods and services.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, A agrees to sell some goods to B and also to deliver them to B. A also agrees to install them upon delivery.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: An engineer agrees to repair B's broken machine and supplies some small spare parts while doing so.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A club allows B to become a member and provides B with both goods (such as books and a special badge) and services (such as advice or the use of club premises) when B joins.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In each of these cases, is there a single supply or more than one supply?

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: States need to adopt simple practical rules for dealing with these everyday occurrences so that those making mixed supplies and multiple supplies can determine without excess difficulty how and when VAT is to be applied to each supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: One broad practical rule is to treat any supplies incidental to a main supply as part of that main supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If, for example, A makes no separate charge for delivery, then the service of delivery is ignored, and the supply is taxed only as a supply of goods.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If the engineer charges separately for the spare parts, then VAT should be applied separately to them.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A multiple supply, such as club membership, may require that the one payment be apportioned between the different elements of club membership.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A simple broad VAT allows many of these problems to be avoided.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If none of the forms of supply is exempt and all are subject to VAT at the same rate, then it is not as critical to separate the elements of a supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: When numerous categories of exemption are allowed and more than one rate of VAT is introduced, administration becomes more complicated because much closer attention must be given to this problem.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: When a Supply of Goods Takes Place The time of supply is important for deciding when a tax invoice has to be issued in respect of a supply, when tax is due in respect of a supply, the rate at which the tax is payable,82 and in which taxable period a return has to be made in respect of that supply and in which any tax credit can be claimed by the person receiving the supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In cases where the rate of tax has been changed from one period to the other.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 28 - The rules determining when a supply of goods takes place vary from one state to another83 but generally a supply of goods takes place when • a VAT invoice is issued for the supply, • the goods are delivered, • the goods are made available, • the goods are removed or transported to or for the customer, or • the goods are paid for in whole or in part.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In accounting terms, these rules include both a cash basis and an accrual basis for timing a transaction.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In the interests of securing the cash-flow position of the state and of ensuring efficient collection of the VAT, it is usual to provide that the time of supply occurs when the first of these events occurs, or soon thereafter.84 Once a VAT system is established, it may be most efficient to provide that the primary rule governing time of supply is that the supply occurs at the time when the VAT invoice is issued, provided that the invoice is issued promptly.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In practice, many suppliers issue tax invoices at the time of a supply or shortly thereafter to comply with the obligation to issue a timely invoice.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The law could, for example, define the time limit as seven days after what would otherwise be the time of supply under the rules set forth above.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A supply of goods is defined as a transfer of the owner's right to dispose of tangible property, but the time of supply for the purposes of this law is fixed not by reference to that transfer, but by reference to the delivery of the goods themselves.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Often, the transfer of the right will occur with the delivery of the goods, but this will depend on the precise provisions of the laws of the state relating to the sale of goods and supplies of other kinds.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Sometimes goods are not "delivered" in the usual meaning of the word.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, a supplier sells to a customer an agreed quantity of a commodity, such as grain.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This applies for invoice-based and transaction-based approaches to VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If the VAT is levied on an accounts base (e.g., in Japan), the timing rules are the same or similar to those applying for corporation tax.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This is often based on general accounting principles and therefore relates either to the cash transaction or to accrual.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: 84 Special considerations may apply in some transition countries where there are serious problems of interenterprise arrears.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Many of these countries operate VAT on a cash basis, or provide that the taxable event occurs at a specified time after the events referred to in the text.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, in Georgia the taxable event occurs 90 days after the date that goods are shipped or services are performed.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A complete discussion of the issues is beyond the scope of this chapter, but some general principles can be stated.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: First, it is critical that the rules for time of supply be identical for the output tax and input tax of a particular taxpayer.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If a taxpayer is allowed to pay output tax on a cash basis, the taxpayer should not receive credit for input tax until the taxpayer makes payment for supplies.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Second, as a general matter, to avoid claims of input tax in advance of output tax being paid, it is best to have a single rule that applies to all taxpayers, perhaps with limited exceptions, such as for small taxpayers.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 29 - in a store by the supplier, who releases the grain only when the customer sells it to a third person, to whom the supplier delivers the goods on demand from the store.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In such a case, not only are the goods not delivered to the customer, but they are not appropriated to the customer either.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Cases such as this could be dealt with in regulations.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Those regulations might be based on the legal provisions of the state dealing with the transfer of ownership of goods in situations where the transfer does not involve delivery.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Where payment is made in advance of goods being delivered, the supply should be considered as taking place on the date of the payment to the extent of its amount.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The aim is to ensure that the VAT liability arises as an advance payment is made and does not await any transfer or dealing with the goods.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Otherwise, advance payments could be used as a means to avoid or delay the payment of VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This may happen, for example, where an advance payment is made, but no invoice is issued.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If the goods are delivered, it may be said to be a loan for which no payment is claimed pending the more formal agreement.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This more formal agreement never occurs, thus leaving the supplier with an advance payment that apparently does not relate to any supply and leaving the person supplied with the use of goods for perhaps a long period.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The reference in the preceding paragraph to a supply taking place to the extent of the amount of the payment implies that where only partial payment is made, portions of the amount of the supply will take place on different dates.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A partial payment is treated as the first occasion of supply and the occasion for any further supplies is determined in accordance with the general rules.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This rule will apply separately to the situation where two or more payments are made for a supply if separate invoices are issued in respect of each payment.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If one invoice is issued for the full amount due, then this will represent the applicable date for the supply for the whole sum, although payment is made in installments.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Where the "supply" of goods is actually a series of supplies occurring on a number of separate occasions, then a taxable supply occurs on each separate occasion.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, a customer may agree to buy from a supplier the right to set up a market stall on the supplier's land each Thursday throughout a year.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A supply of the use of land in this way is a taxable supply of services.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Is it one supply or a supply of the use of the land each Thursday?

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A technical answer to this question might refer to the precise terms of the contract under which the supplier agrees to supply the use of land in this way, including the method of payment adopted.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Treating each date of supply as a separate supply achieves an efficient and practical result in that the supply is regarded as occurring each Thursday if payment is made for each week only after that week.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If payment is made for the whole year at a set time before the end of the year, the rule about prior payment will apply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It is normally appropriate to apply the rules by reference to the terms of the agreement between the supplier and the customer.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: To avoid practical problems and to simplify administration, regulations can deal in detail with cases such as this.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: J. When a Supply of Services Takes Place Tax Law Design and Drafting (volume 1; International Monetary Fund: 1996; Victor Thuronyi, ed.)

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 30 - The considerations set out as applying to the time when a supply of goods takes place also largely apply to a supply of services.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: However, services are not "delivered" or "appropriated" in the same way as goods.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Instead, it is usual to determine the time of supply by reference to when the services have been rendered.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This is a question of fact to be interpreted in the light of any contract or agreement under which the services are supplied.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A special case that may need a different rule is that of a supply of services over a long period or a continuing supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If a supplier agrees to supply a customer with a continuing service (e.g., a telephone service, a supply of electricity, or continuing professional assistance), the supply might be regarded as never reaching the point at which it "is performed" until the contract between the supplier and the customer is ended, or it might be viewed as provided every minute, which would be impractical.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: However, payment is made from time to time, and the rule about partial payment can be applied.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Alternatively, it may be that the contract between the supplier and the customer shows that the services are supplied, in effect, on a series of separate occasions.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If so, it is usual to treat each supply as made when a partial payment for the supply is made or when an invoice is issued for that part.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It may be that the "supply" is not one supply, but a series of supplies.

meta.creator: Unknown

text: If cases of difficulty arise under this general rule, special provision can be made through regulation.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The introduction to this chapter stressed that the VAT is usually based on the destination principle, that is, with goods being subject to VAT where they are either received or consumed.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For this reason, goods crossing frontiers are subject to a regime similar to customs duties on arrival.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Therefore, it is necessary to clarify where goods are received.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In the case of imported goods, the adoption of customs laws will help deal with this problem.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The VAT laws can adopt from the customs laws rules to determine when goods are imported and the nature of the goods imported.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In practice, most international supplies of goods are caught in this way by the customs laws of states.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Location rules may also be useful within the state and to deal with exports.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Often, a general rule is included in the law to locate a supply of goods where the goods are delivered or made available to the person supplied, in other words, where they are physically handed over.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The fact that legal title does not pass at that time is not the important issue.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For goods that are being transported, a rule is needed to determine whether they are delivered at the start or at the end of the transportation.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A rule that goods are delivered where the transportation starts will accord with the common commercial arrangement that goods are at the risk of the buyer while being transported.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It will also ensure that the location of the supply of goods being exported is within the state.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: That is necessary to provide a legal basis for providing a rebate of VAT on inputs used to produce those goods.

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 31 - Determining the location of a supply of services can be a matter of considerable difficulty, especially for international services.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Customs rules cannot be used because they do not apply to services.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A second difficulty arises from the application of the destination principle.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This provides that services should be taxed where they are received or consumed.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: However, consider, for example, the supply of legal services by a lawyer in one country to a person in another country.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The physical location of the supply may be both difficult to determine and irrelevant to the place where the supply is consumed.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It might take place in the country of the lawyer, that of the client, in some third state, on an aircraft, over the telephone, or through e-mail originating in, or received in, a range of offices.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If the law firm has offices in several states, the advice could be sent from any of those states.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The underlying legal research, writing, and investigation could also be performed in a variety of places.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Behind those problems lies that of ensuring that a taxable person is within the jurisdiction of the state, so that the VAT can be enforced.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This does not matter for imported goods, because in the last resort the goods themselves provide security for payment of the VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Equally, it is easy to identify a person who can be treated as importer, and duties may be imposed on that person.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Another policy aspect is that fairness and neutrality require that services that originate overseas be taxed in the same way as services that originate in the state.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Otherwise, overseas suppliers may be able to compete on unfair terms.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In the absence of any international agreement setting jurisdictional limits to VAT and any ready assistance in enforcing VAT in other states, there is no clear and universally accepted answer to the question of how to treat international services.85

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Some aspects of the problem can be solved by identifying separate rules for particular kinds of supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, where the services relate to land or other immovable property, it is common to treat the services as supplied where the land is situated.86 This provides a rule consistent with usual rules on conflicts of laws, and also access to security.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Similarly, a supply of transport services can be treated as occurring where the transport is supplied.87 85 The EC adopted standard rules in 1977 but was unable to adopt a simple and universal rule.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: As will be noted further in the text, the main rule relates to the supplier's place of business, but there are four sets of exceptions to this, two of which are permissive rather than mandatory.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: As a result, the location rules within the EU member states are not entirely consistent.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 32 - Beyond this, states tend to adopt rules that locate a supply at a place of business either of the supplier or of the customer.88 The practical problem about locating the supply where the customer is located is imposing the VAT on that supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A reverse-charging rule treats the customer being supplied with a service originating abroad as making the supply to itself.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It must then account to its tax authorities for the VAT due as output tax on that supply.89

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: However, if the customer makes exempt supplies, then no VAT credit or deduction is available.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: M. Treatment of Imports The destination principle requires a charge to VAT to be placed on all imports.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This is usually done through a charging provision that parallels the one on internal supplies.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The parallel provision normally adopts and adapts the laws imposing customs duties on the imported goods.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The laws determining whether items are goods (inclusion in the tariff), whether they are imported (rules of origin), and when and where they are imported will serve for VAT purposes as for customs duty purposes, although it may be necessary to make clear that the act of importing occurs within the territory of the state for VAT purposes to avoid any legal problems.90 Customs regimes, such as free ports, duty-free shops, and tax-free zones can be applied readily to VAT on this basis, the zones being regarded as outside the territory of the state.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Taxable Supplies A. Definition 88The primary rule in the European Union is that the service is supplied "where the supplier has established his business or has a fixed establishment . . .

meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 33 - A "taxable supply" is a supply or transaction on which VAT is imposed.91 When a taxable supply is made, the person making the supply, if a taxable person, must impose and collect VAT and account for it to the tax authorities.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Even if the person does not do this, the tax authorities are still entitled to collect VAT from the taxable person on the assumption that the VAT had been imposed.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The law should impose it on all supplies of goods and services within the scope of VAT and made by a taxable person unless the law itself exempts the supply from VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: As previously noted, to be within the scope of VAT, a supply of goods and services must also be made (a) as part of the economic activities of the supplier, and (b) against payment (or for consideration) to that person from some other person.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: To complete the full definition of taxable supplies, the law must also therefore define both these criteria and determine the extent of exemption.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: B. text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 35 - C. Payment for a Supply A supply is made for payment, consideration, or compensation98 if the taxable person making the supply receives, or is entitled to receive, payment for the supply.99 For this purpose, it does not matter in what form the payment is made.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

meta.creator: Unknown

meta.creator: Unknown

text: Broad policy considerations, including ease of administration, the revenue levels produced by VAT compared with other taxes, the trade-off between the rate structure of VAT and the base on which those rates are levied (the broader the base, the lower the rates), fairness, and economic neutrality of the tax, all argue for minimal use of exemptions.110 Political considerations in individual states and, in particular, the political perception of social considerations have been used to argue to introduce or preserve exemptions.

text: A few states have distorted the VAT framework even further by allowing zero rating of internal supplies.112 As discussed below,113 zero rating of exports and international supplies is very common.

meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 40 - B. Effect of Exemptions

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It is often assumed that "exemption" results in the reduction of the VAT burden on a supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This is true if the person supplied is a consumer and is not receiving the supply as part of a business.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It is not true if the person supplied is a taxable person.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Exemption of a supply to a business results in an increase in the burden of VAT on the supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The reason for this is that the person running the business can offset the VAT against the VAT charged by the business, so claiming a full rebate for any VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The person making the exempt supply will probably have had to pay VAT on some part of the supplies made to it and will therefore have to pass some VAT on to the business as part of its price.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It is this VAT that can be recovered if the supply is subject to tax, but that cannot be recovered if it is exempt.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: To avoid the distortions caused by this failure to recover, it is good policy not to exempt the types of supply that are typically made to business.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Although there are strong policy arguments for minimizing exemptions, no state has succeeded in removing all exemptions from the law.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Even New Zealand, which has been most successful in curbing the extent of exemptions, has maintained some.114 1.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Land and Buildings Transactions involving land and buildings are commonly exempted.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: As previously noted, many states provide that a sale of land, or other transfer of the title to land, is outside the scope of VAT.

meta.creator: Unknown

text: Other states achieve the same effect by exempting these supplies.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Further, the law needs to deal with supplies of services related to land.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The main service is the use of land, or leases or tenancies of land.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For the same reason that land itself is exempted, it is common to find that leases and lettings of land are also exempted.115 At the same time, there is no strong reason for exempting commercial uses of immovable property, such as accommodation in a hotel.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This may be done by excluding categories of land use (such as holiday use) from the exemption or by setting a minimum time period for exempt leases and tenancies (perhaps two months).116 114 The New Zealand exemptions are (in summary) financial services, certain supplies by nonprofit bodies, certain supplies of accommodation and land, and supplies of gold and fine metals.

text: Supplies by Nonprofit Organizations and Individuals Many states provide exemptions for social goods and services, that is, supplies that are made to individuals and that do not form, or do not usually form, business supplies.

meta.creator: Unknown

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Many social supplies are outside the scope of VAT because they are not made as part of a business or are not made for payment or consideration (as with free health supplies from a state authority).

text: D. Using Alternative Taxes The exclusion of categories of supply from the scope of VAT, or the exemption of those categories, does not mean that those supplies need be excluded from all indirect taxation.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It is noticeable that states, finding it less practicable to impose a VAT on forms of internal and international supply, are increasingly adopting other taxes to make good the revenue loss.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Examples of internal supplies taxed in this way are taxation of transactions involving land and buildings by imposing stamp duties or transaction taxes or high registration fees on the documents used for the transfers; exemption of insurance services, but the imposition instead of taxes on insurance policies or premiums; use of income taxes and other direct taxes to ensure taxation of payments for financial services (particularly interest) in place of the almost universal exemption from VAT of those services; exemption from VAT for betting and gaming, offset by specific taxes on those activities; exemption of activities where there is a state monopoly (e.g., postal services and some transport services), with fiscal adjustments to prices being used to the same effect.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Examples also occur of taxes being imposed on those international supplies that are exempted or zero rated by reason of the destination principle or pressures of competition.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: An increasingly common example is taxation of airports and airline tickets.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Another is tourist taxes of various kinds, such as exit taxes when tourists leave the state.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Further discussion of this topic is beyond the scope of this chapter.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: E. Exemption of Diplomatic Activities States generally have accepted treaty obligations to exempt certain supplies or imports as part of the recognition of diplomatic and consular immunities and of similar immunities for 120 Several states have considered the taxation of financial services in detail, including New Zealand, Canada, and the United States, but found themselves unable to resolve satisfactorily the practical and conceptual problems raised by this charge to tax.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: There is an unresolved disagreement between experts about whether, and to what extent, interest should be subject to VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It is argued by some that the whole interest should be included in the potential charge to VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 43 - international organizations.121 These involve immunity from taxation for the embassies and consulates and for the recognized diplomats and consuls.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: These immunities are normally operated on a reciprocal basis and are based on the provisions of the international conventions that set out the required immunity from taxation.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In many states, no express provision is included in the VAT law on this matter, because the exemption is provided under the terms of international obligations that are part of national law.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If such obligations are not self-executing in a particular country, or if the country wishes to clarify or expand on the exemptions accorded, a specific exemption needs to be provided in the VAT law.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: F. Exempt Imports International practice recognizes agreed categories of goods that are exempted from customs duty on import.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Practice on this is well established and ranges from the import of a limited quantity of goods bought duty free in other states to exemption of gifts to charities or similar organizations.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It is for consideration how far those exemptions should also apply for VAT purposes.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Some are appropriate because of the underlying reason for the exemption from customs duty.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Others would not be appropriate because they would create unfair competition with those supplying similar goods from within the state.122 Principles of fairness and efficiency argue for minimal exemption from VAT even where customs duty exemptions apply, particularly if there is a business purpose behind the import.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Whatever the policy adopted, it is convenient in most cases to frame the VAT exemptions on imports with the customs duty exemptions in mind, so as to avoid unnecessary inconsistencies.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: One particular category of import has caused particular concern in developing states and the economies in transition.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This is the import of foreign-produced machinery and equipment for the use of local businesses.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In principle, such items should be subject to VAT when imported, if also subject to VAT when produced locally.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In some states, there is no local capacity to produce such items, and importers lobby strongly for VAT exemption.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The imposition of VAT would not be much of a problem for taxpayers if a credit for the tax were immediately allowed, but there are often restrictions on such credits (e.g., a delayed credit for capital goods, a requirement to carry over excess credits, or a de facto difficulty in obtaining refunds).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If an exemption is granted for pragmatic reasons, it should be restricted in scope and time and conditional on the genuine business use of the equipment.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: G. Problems Caused by Exempt Supplies 121 The main treaties are the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, Apr. 18, 1961; the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations, Apr. 24, 1963; and the agreements and conventions relating to individual international organizations.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The exemption often takes the form of zero rating.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, an exemption on the import of manufactured goods will distort competition with any similar goods produced internally unless they are also exempt.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: There are, however, only limited circumstances in which it may be appropriate to exempt the domestic production of manufactured goods.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 44 - While, as discussed above, for both political and technical reasons it may be necessary to exempt a number of different types of supplies, exemptions create significant distortions beyond those that may be obvious (i.e., the fact that certain supplies to final consumers are favored over others).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: One of these distortions—the problem of exempt supplies made to businesses that are VAT taxpayers—has already been discussed above.123 Another important problem is that of input credits to a business that makes both taxable and exempt supplies.124 That problem involves the conceptual and practical difficulty of determining which inputs are attributable to exempt supplies.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Inputs to exempt supplies cause an additional problem; namely, they create an incentive for a person making exempt supplies to supply itself through its own employees, instead of purchasing inputs from others.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, a bank whose supplies are entirely or largely exempt financial services may enter into a contract with a security company to provide security guards.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The security company will charge VAT to the bank if it is a taxable person, and the bank will be unable to recover the VAT as an imput credit.125

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The bank would have an incentive to hire security guards as its own employees.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Because employee services are outside the VAT, this maneuver quite legally minimizes the bank's tax costs.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In response, some states have imposed VAT in certain cases of self-supply by taxpayers.126 However, antiabuse rules of this kind are of necessity limited in scope and cannot be generalized unless the VAT is fundamentally restructured (such as by treating all employee services as taxable).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In addition to such legal avoidance, exemption leads to temptation for evasion: while normally businesses do not have an incentive to avoid VAT on their supplies (except as part of a scheme of tax evasion that would also involve the understatement of sales), a person making exempt supplies has an incentive to pay its suppliers under the table.127 Widespread exemptions can therefore undermine the integrity of the VAT as a whole.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This is a consequence of the invoice-credit method of VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The method works reasonably well if all supplies are taxable, but starts to break down when some supplies in a chain are exempt.

meta.creator: Unknown

meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 45 - VAT is designed as a tax levied as a proportion of the value added on any taxable supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It is therefore necessary to attribute a value (referred to as "the value"128) to all taxable supplies to ensure that this objective is achieved.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: To be consistent with the fundamental principles of the tax, the value to be taxed must reflect the value added by the supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: B. Value of Internal Supplies The general rule for valuing a supply for VAT purposes is to value it at the total of all payments, or consideration, that the supplier receives or is entitled to receive as a result of the supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In other words, the value is taken as the actual realized value.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This relates to the requirement, already discussed, that there be payment for a supply in most cases for it to be within the scope of VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: All forms of payment or consideration, whether paid by the person supplied or some other person, are relevant for that purpose.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: They are also relevant in determining the total value.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For the purposes of the general rule, it is irrelevant whether the total payment represents a "good" or a "bad" price for the supply, as long as it is a genuine price and not a sham.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It is common to find rules that displace the price paid in certain cases, but in most commercial transactions it is a matter of indifference to the tax authorities if the price is "too" high or low.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This is because any distortion of the price is neutralized if both the supplier and the person supplied are fully taxable persons.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Any increase or decrease in the VAT collected will then be offset by a similar increase or decrease in the VAT credit or input tax deduction claimed.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The matter is only of concern if the high or low price increases the overall amount of input tax available for deduction or decreases the overall collection of output tax.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This will happen only where one party is a taxable person and the other is not.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The value of a supply should be taken as including all other taxes paid on that supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: VAT is not an alternative form of excise tax or customs duty, but is a separate tax.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Both customs duties and excise taxes reflect the state's separate decisions to increase the price of the dutiable and excisable products by the amount of the duty or tax.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: That represents the value of final consumption of the goods for VAT purposes and is therefore the basis of the value for VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If it is felt that the combined effect of excise duty and VAT on a product is too high, the answer lies in adjusting the level of excise duty, not of the VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This is not only consistent with principle, but is also both simpler to administer and less distortionary.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The alternatives would 128 “Value" is the simplest English term (and is used, for example, in New Zealand, NZL GST § 4, and the United Kingdom, GBR VAT § 19), although "taxable amount" is also used in the Basic World Tax Code, Hussey & Lubick, supra note 13, § 221.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 46 - either be to exempt the items from VAT if subject to duty or to calculate the VAT on the price without counting the duty.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Both would add significantly to the overall administrative burden on suppliers and the tax authority for no fiscal purpose.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The law should state that the value does not include the VAT itself.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Otherwise, a circular element is introduced into the calculation.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The amount paid by the customer for a supply may be defined as including or excluding the VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In some states, it is assumed in such a case that the VAT is to be added to that price, so that the full amount paid by the customer is 100 plus VAT.129

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In other states the assumption is the reverse of this, namely, that if the price is stated as "100," then that is the total that the customer is obliged to pay, including VAT.130 In the first case, the value of the supply is, as defined above, 100.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In the second case, the value plus the VAT is 100.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, if the rate of VAT is 10 percent, then in this case the value is 90.9, and the VAT payable is 9.1 (rounded to the nearest decimal point).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The decision whether to include or exclude the VAT in determining the relationship between the value and the total consideration will need to be taken into account in framing the VAT law.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: However, it is a rule that belongs to the commercial law or consumer law of the state, not the VAT law.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Any measure penalizing the exploitation of the rule to overcharge customers also belongs in a law other than the VAT law.

text: D. Fair Market Value of Supply Where the person supplied is not a taxable person, or not a fully taxable person, but the supplier is a fully taxable person in respect of the supply, there may be a temptation for taxpayers to understate the price to avoid creating input tax that the person supplied cannot reclaim.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: There are also cases131 where a supply is treated as being made for payment, even though nothing is paid or payable.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In both cases, it may be considered appropriate to override the general rule.132 Instead, value would be based on an independent measure of the value added by the transaction.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This would normally be the open market price, or arm's-length price, of the supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Again, clear rules will be needed to apply an alternative basis of valuation.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Temptation to adjust prices may also arise in the case of mixed supplies or supplies where a number of different parties are involved.

meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, where a taxable person is acting on behalf of someone else, those transactions undertaken as agent for the other person may not 129 This is the standard approach taken with regard to sales taxes in the United States.

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 47 - be subject to VAT because the principal is not a taxable person.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Here, close attention needs to be paid to ensuring that the total payment is shared properly between the different parts of the total transaction.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This does not require the total payment to be altered.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It will also be needed in any other case where the law allows the tax authorities to override or ignore the actual price.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Put at its broadest, the power to override may be justified in any case where the relationship between the supplier and the person supplied is such that the price fixed between them may be open to pressures other than market pressures and where one or both parties are not fully taxable persons in respect of the supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This will, for instance, include transactions between related persons.

text: More generally, this issue can be addressed through legislative provisions similar to those found in income tax law (and customs law).133 E. Adjustments and Rebates

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The rules to determine value need to be simple and easy to apply at the moment of sale, without delay or difficulty.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: They are applied in millions of transactions by everyone actually making supplies and fixing prices.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Save for specifically documented adjustments, the person making the sale or supply must be able to determine what figures to put on the VAT invoice at that time without any need to revise them.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The rules determining value must therefore deal clearly with any adjustments, such as discounts, made to prices.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, if goods are sold as "normally 100, but 90 for today only," what is the price?

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The answer is that today the price is 90, that is, the value actually added by the transaction.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: However, tomorrow, it is 100, unless the lower price is actually agreed upon.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For this reason, the value should be the price after any discounts.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The position is more difficult if the price for a sale is "100, but only 95 if you pay within seven days."

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In this case, the customer might pay either 95 or 100, and the supplier does not know at the time of sale.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Here, the usual practice is to take the lower price, which is all that the customer needs to pay.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The extra 5 might be regarded as a fee for late payment (and as such might be regarded as payment for an exempt financial service).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Another complication is the use of vouchers or tokens.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, a person buys an item at a shop and pays the full price, but also receives a voucher good for a reduction of 10 in the price on purchase of a second item.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The sale of the second item will then be discounted to this person, even though others pay the full 133 This topic, together with the problems of definition within it (such as the problem of defining a market price), is of considerable concern in the income tax.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It links, in particular, to the problem of transfer pricing.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This topic receives thorough discussion elsewhere (see vol. 2, ch. 18) and is not covered further here.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The value added, in the case of the sale to this person, is always the discounted price.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This is both consistent with the principles of the tax and the most practical answer.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Further complications arise where the effect of a discount, or an arrangement on purchase, results in a later adjustment.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In this case, no account should be taken of the change in connection with the first transaction.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This should be dealt with as a separate transaction and treated in the same way for administrative reasons as a separate supply, even if the supplier pays money to the person supplied and therefore reduces the net consideration.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: When the adjustment occurs, the VAT should be added, or rebated, in exactly the same way as on the original supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It is important from the point of view of the tax administration that there be no reason to alter the VAT invoice issued in connection with a transaction.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Once the VAT invoice is issued, there should be no provision allowing for its alteration, except for the correction of an error.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, if a customer pays $1,000 and an invoice is issued for $100, then a corrected invoice should be issued upon discovery of the mistake.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: F. Value of Imports In the special case of imports of goods, it is standard practice to use the customs value of goods as the value for VAT, subject to specific adjustments.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The "customs value" generally represents an internationally agreed upon approach to the valuation of goods subject to customs duty and therefore minimizes the scope for difficulty or dispute in levying VAT on the import.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It also simplifies the operation of VAT on imported goods and allows the VAT to be calculated at the same time as the customs duty and by the same officials.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The customs approach may also be used when fixing the value for VAT of goods exempted from customs duty but liable to VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Attention has already been drawn to the advisability of aligning as far as appropriate the VAT exemptions on imports with the exemptions that apply under the customs code.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Two standard adjustments are needed to convert the customs value of goods to the value for VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: First, consistent with the policy discussed previously on internal supplies, the value for VAT should include the customs duty itself.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Excises levied on imports should likewise be added to the VAT base.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Second, the customs duty will usually include all freight and handling charges and similar costs to bring the goods into customs control.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The obligation on the person delivering the goods to the state may include further charges and the cost of inland freight to the place of delivery within the state.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If the goods are not handed over at the time or place of customs clearance, then the value for VAT should include all additional freighting and other charges incurred up to the time of delivery to the customer.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This is, again, consistent with the approach taken on internal supplies.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If these extra charges are separate, then they may need to be dealt with as separate supplies.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Payment of VAT A. Determining the Amount to Be Paid Tax Law Design and Drafting (volume 1; International Monetary Fund: 1996; Victor Thuronyi, ed.)

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 49 - Two important elements remain in order to establish how much VAT the taxable person must pay to the tax authorities.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The first is the rate of VAT to be paid on the value of any supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This, together with issues already discussed, deals completely with the question of determining the output tax on any supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The second is the offset of input tax against output tax to identify the net VAT payable.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: These topics, and associated issues, are discussed in this section.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: B. Rates of VAT Countries' practices in setting the rate or rates of VAT have varied widely over the forty years since the tax was first introduced.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Some countries have imposed six or more effective rates at the same time.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The result has been some confusion as to the purpose of the tax and considerable administrative complexity and market distortion.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Recognition of these problems, and of the underlying policy issues, has led states to abandon complex rate structures.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A detailed discussion of the relevant policy issues is beyond the scope of this chapter.134 However, recent practice may be noted, and best practice commended.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It is now generally accepted that the VAT should not be used as a vehicle for imposing luxury rates of indirect tax.135 If a state wishes to impose high rates of indirect tax on specific goods or services, then the generally easier way to do so is with a separate excise duty or tax.136

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Internally, it simplifies the identification of luxury goods.
