meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Internationally, it avoids any accusation that differential rates of VAT are being used for discriminatory purposes.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It follows from this that VAT will have a main or basic rate and one or more lower rates.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The main rate of VAT is an important matter of fiscal policy in any state and the level varies significantly among states.137 134 See Tait, supra note 2, ch. 2. 135

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This is expressly excluded within the European Union.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Several EU states that used to impose luxury rates of VAT have therefore withdrawn them.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Some African countries still use luxury rates (in some cases first introduced following the French example, although France itself has since adopted the EU rules).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: An interesting example of a VAT-style tax being expressly geared at luxury items is the Wholesale and Luxury Tax in Venezuela.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The VEN IC is levied at a standard rate and at two additional luxury rates.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The additional rates are applied to items such as cars, tobacco, jewelry, and cable TV.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In making such a decision, however, one would have to bear in mind the manufacturing process for the goods in question and, accordingly, the suitability of excise administrative procedures compared with procedures under the VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The European Union has agreed upon a minimum main rate of 15 percent, and rates vary from that to 25 percent in Europe.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Elsewhere, countries with very broad forms of VAT can afford lower rates (such as New Zealand, NZL GST § 8(1)(rate of 12.5 percent)), while states under fiscal pressure have had rates of 30 percent or above.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 50 - Clearly, the higher the main rate, the more pressure there will be from lobby groups to apply one or more lower rates to specific items.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In practice, it should be remembered that no long-term social objective is achieved by setting any rate other than the main rate on goods or services supplied to fully taxable persons.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: There may be a cash-flow advantage to them in not having to pay quite so much VAT before making a claim for the VAT credit for deductible input tax, but in the longer run the VAT they pay is reclaimed against their own output tax as a VAT credit for input tax and thus has no residual effect.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Arguments for lower rates therefore concentrate on socially important goods such as food, and socially important services that are not exempted or outside the scope of VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Of course, there is a cost in VAT forgone in allowing a lower rate, and any lower rate will usually cause either the main rate of VAT to be higher than it otherwise would be, or other taxes to be higher, given the total tax revenue.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Some states have decided that it is better to collect VAT at one rate and to deal with such pressures in other ways (through subsidies or adjustments in social security entitlements), while others have opted for a lower rate.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Again, practice used to involve a range of lower rates but has tended to simplify toward one lower rate (as is happening within the European Union) or none.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In addition to the main rate of VAT and any lower rates, it is normal practice for states to have a zero rate of tax, although it may not be called this.138 A zero rate means that, while no VAT is due on the supply, the supplier remains entitled to claim any input tax incurred in making that supply and is therefore entitled to a refund of that input tax if there is no output tax against which to offset the input tax.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The zero rate is sometimes known as exemption with credit.139 Both terms are correct, depending on the approach taken to exemption and the structure of the tax.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: From one point of view, a tax rate of 0 percent is nonsense.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A zero rate is therefore an exemption of the supply from output tax.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A contrary argument is that in taxes with progressive rate schedules, a zero rate of tax is commonly found at the bottom bracket, so this is not a contradictory concept.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The effect of a zero rate is approximately the same as that of a very low positive rate of tax.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In any event, a zero rate does 138 "Zero rate" has become the usual English-language term, except in EU documents.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It is used, for example by Tait, supra note 2, ch. 3, and Hussey & Lubick, supra note 13, § 222; and in IRL VAT Second Schedule; NZL GST § 11; ZAF VAT § 11; GBR VAT § 30; KAZ TC arts.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: 62–66. (There is inconsistency in the use of the hyphen—both "zero rating" and "zero-rating" are found.)

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The French CGI, art. 261, addresses "opérations exonérées," and this term is followed in the Swiss law.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Technically, in EU law, the requirement is that states exempt the supplies that are discussed here as zero rated.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: However, a separate provision grants a right of deduction for input tax.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It is the form followed in most EU countries and elsewhere in Europe, for instance in Bulgaria.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 51 - make the supply "taxable" in a technical sense and therefore achieves the objective of bringing these transactions within the operation of the VAT credit for input tax, which an exemption does not.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This is because a VAT credit is allowed only for inputs to be used in making taxable supplies.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For this reason, those who do not accept the existence of the zero rate recognize the right to the credit for input tax by saying that these supplies are "exempt with credit."

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: There are arguments in favor of both approaches, and the present writer will readily confess to regarding both as entirely proper ways of defining the process.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The question is one of terminology, and the appropriate solution may depend on the language and practice of a particular state.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: D. Zero Rating Exports and International Supplies Why do states have a zero rate?

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Its main use is to deal with exports of goods and exported supplies of international services.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The destination principle calls not only for removing a direct charge to VAT from exports and international services, but also for removing any VAT indirectly imposed on those supplies in the form of input tax paid by a supplier.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Only if the input tax is rebated will the goods leave the state free of VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The arguments about zero rating exports are also sometimes applied to supplies to diplomats, which are typically zero rated.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The justification is that embassies are to be regarded as outside the tax territory of the state.140 Another specific service that is often zero rated is the supply of international transport.141 The zero rating is usually widely drawn to cover both the supply of the services themselves and also supporting supplies of goods and services (e.g., selling provisions to shipping or repairing an aircraft).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This is often done to protect international transport businesses based in the state from uneven competition from other states.142 For example, two companies, one based in state A and the other in state B, supply bus services between cities in state A and state B.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If state A zero rates the transport supplies, and state B does not, there will be a strong inducement for passengers to travel with state A's company.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In addition, if tickets for the state B company are sold in state A, they may also be zero rated.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: An alternative approach of taxing the services in state B, but not beyond B's frontier, might be theoretically attractive but will pose practical difficulties.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Some states have adopted the alternative approach of imposing a separate excise tax on the tickets provided for international transportation.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Coordinating rules will be needed to deal with supplies that fall under both exemption and zero rating.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, if medical supplies are generally exempt, what about an export of 140 See supra sec. V(E) (discussing the exemption of diplomatic activities).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This applies throughout the European Union and elsewhere in Europe.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It is easier for island states, such as New Zealand, to avoid this problem because the competition is less severe.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It also avoids problems for some states that have goods transiting across them between third states.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The transport service is supplied in the state, but none of the parties involved need have any contact with it (save for the presence of the vehicle and cargo during transit).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 52 - medical supplies?

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Such an export should be treated the same as exports generally, for example, by excluding from the category of exempt transactions those that fall under zero rating.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This is widely viewed as inappropriate, because it amounts to a subsidy of the activity or transaction treated in this way.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It would usually be better to identify the policy reason for the subsidy and address it through a direct subsidy.143its activities is zero rated than is in fact the case.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: On the other hand, one aspect of zero rating is more consistent with the structure of the VAT: unlike exemptions, zero rating does not provide an incentive for suppliers to avoid input tax.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A few special cases exist where zero rating may be justified on internal supplies, notwithstanding the above point.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: One case is of monetary supplies made to the national bank of the state.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Failure to protect the national bank from a charge to VAT on all supplies of gold to it may result in taxing the national reserves.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Similarly, it is normally regarded as appropriate to protect supplies of the currency itself to the central bank from the imposition of VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This will have to be done in any event in some way, and the simplest way is through zero rating.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Other financial supplies are of course likely to be exempt.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Another special case is that of the sale or other transfer of an ongoing business.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The problem arises when a taxable person transfers a business activity to another taxable person.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Strictly, the seller must treat the sale of the business as subject to VAT (usually at the main rate).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The buyer must therefore pay, along with the purchase price, the VAT on that price.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If the purchaser is also a taxable person in respect of that business, then the purchaser can claim back the whole of the VAT paid as a credit for input tax.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: However, the associated credit or refund may take some time to receive, depending on the rules in the state dealing with large rebates of input tax.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: There are therefore significant potential cash-flow problems for the purchaser even though, in the long run, the input tax can be recovered.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For the tax authorities, the sale of an ongoing business presents no problem.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The VAT is accounted for from the business before and after the sale in the same way.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In the long run, therefore, the sale will involve no additional VAT or loss of VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: To avoid this short-term problem, and recognizing that in the long run there is no revenue significance in this kind of sale, some states provide that such sales or transfers are zero rated.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This means that the transaction remains taxable and does not distort any claims for input tax by 143 As discussed in sec. V(G) supra, there are similar problems with using exemptions.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If it is determined to provide a VAT preference rather than a direct subsidy, the question arises whether the preference should take the form of exemption or of zero rating.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It can also be unwise as a political matter, because it would open the door for arguments to zero rate other internal supplies.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Zero rating also leads to administrative problems, in that a supplier may claim that a greater portion of Tax Law Design and Drafting (volume 1; International Monetary Fund: 1996; Victor Thuronyi, ed.)

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Other states remove the transaction by taking it outside the scope of VAT, but in this case an adjustment may need to be made to deal with the problem of input tax.144 F.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Paying VAT to the Tax Authorities The law must establish a mechanism for each taxable person to account for the VAT collected by that person on sales, and to pay this tax over to the tax authorities at regular intervals, after deduction of any allowable input tax.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The procedures for doing this are noted briefly in the next section.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The element of substantive law involved is the right to claim a deduction for input tax.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If a sale or other transfer of an ongoing business is taken outside the scope of VAT, then it must be provided that the business is treated as continuing regardless of the change of owner to prevent a break in the flow of output tax and claims for input tax and also to prevent any claims by the new owner for input tax already credited to the former owner.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 54 - G. Entitlement to Credit for Input Tax145

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It follows from the definition of "value added" on which VAT is based that any VAT incurred by a taxable person as input tax should be repaid to that person in some way.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The usual method of repayment is to allow the input tax to be set off as a deduction or credit146 against output tax collected during the same period.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A duty is imposed on the taxable person to pay only the net amount to the tax authorities.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In principle, therefore, all relevant input tax incurred by a taxable person should be available for credit in this way.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: While the mechanism for crediting input tax presents few difficulties for taxable persons who make only taxable supplies (or exempt supplies that carry a right of credit), two sets of problems arise in particular cases.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The first is that of the person who makes both taxable supplies and other supplies (either exempt supplies or supplies outside the scope of VAT).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The second is the need to safeguard the award of input tax credit against fraud and transactions that may cause revenue loss to the state by avoidance or evasion.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In addition, many states have, partly to deal with the second problem, made provision in the law disallowing credit for some kinds of input tax.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Further, credit of input tax on capital goods is sometimes limited and spread over a period of years.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: 145 Here again, there is inconsistent terminology in different VAT laws.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The use of "output tax" (meaning the VAT imposed by the supplier on taxable supplies made by the supplier) and "input tax" (meaning VAT paid by the supplier) is now widespread in English-speaking countries, but it is by no means universal.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The terms are used by Tait, supra note 2, but not in Hussey & Lubick, supra note 13, which uses the term "input credit."

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: "Input tax" is a defined term in the laws of New Zealand, NZL GST § 2(1); South Africa, ZAF VAT § 1(xxix); and the United Kingdom, GBR VAT § 24, but is not found in the EC Sixth VAT Directive, supra note 3, which focuses on tax for which the right of deduction has arisen.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The Swiss law refers to a right of deduction for the "previous tax" (impôt préalable).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The French law is not as consistent, referring to a deduction for the VAT "imposed on the elements of the price of a taxable operation", see FRA CGI art.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: 271, and in another place to a "deduction for the tax imposed on the goods or services which are not used exclusively for the realization of taxable operations.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The lack of a precise term in the statute is perhaps due to the fact that the operative rules for input tax are left to regulations.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The term in the German law is Vorsteuer, which could be translated as advance tax.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Again, there is inconsistent use of terminology about whether the input tax is available for deduction or credit.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: We have noted that the EU laws refer to a right of deduction.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The alternative form is to refer to a "tax credit" or "VAT credit."

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The latter term is, in the view of this writer, slightly preferable because it emphasizes that the input tax may exceed the output tax (and, at the extreme, that there may be input tax when there is no output tax), so that the "deduction" exceeds the sum from which it is deducted.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This gives rise to an excess deduction or, better, an excess credit.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It also helps to emphasize that there should be a credit (or deduction) for all VAT incurred by the supplier for business purposes.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Direct tax laws impose strict controls on deductions, and such thinking sometimes erroneously strays into VAT laws.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 55 - H. Partial Exemption

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The main category of taxable person with problems in identifying the amounts of input tax available for credit is businesses that make some taxable supplies and some exempt supplies.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: These are often termed cases of partial exemption.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The problem is the same for those that make supplies outside the scope of the tax.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If a state has many exemptions from VAT, or has a limited base for the tax, these problems will be common.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If a state exempts goods of a kind available for retail purchase, then a shop or business that sells these goods and other goods will be partially exempt.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Most states exempt financial services; consequently, banks and other suppliers of financial services routinely confront the problems of partial exemption.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, a finance house makes supplies of financial services, which are exempt, and also supplies business advice that is subject to VAT at the main rate.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The finance house is a heavy user of telephones and incurs a substantial amount of VAT on its telephone bills.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If the finance house were allowed to claim all the input tax on its telephone bills, it would be receiving excessive input tax.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The law therefore allows the finance house to claim the VAT on the telephone bills that relate to its business advice services but not to its financial services.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The law must limit the right to claim a credit so that it covers only input tax incurred for the purposes of making taxable supplies.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This requires a careful review of the total input tax paid by a partially exempt taxable person to separate out that input tax that is to be allowed and that which is not.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: There is no quick but entirely accurate way of doing this.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The principles are that input tax incurred only for the purpose of making taxable supplies is allowed, but input tax incurred only for some other purpose or purposes should not be allowed.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Input tax incurred partly for the purpose of making taxable supplies and partly for other purposes should be apportioned so that only the part of the supply devoted to making taxable supplies is available for credit.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: There are significant practical problems in attempting to divide each item of input tax in this way, and a variety of solutions have been adopted in practice, such as averaging or estimating or generalizing from a partial audit of input tax.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, the rules may be applied strictly for a trial period.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: During this period, the taxable person is required to identify any input tax paid on supplies acquired solely for the purpose of making taxable supplies, any input tax paid in connection with making supplies that are exempt, and the input tax to be apportioned.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The input tax is apportioned in proportion to the total of taxable supplies and the total of exempt supplies (and, depending on how the law is structured, supplies outside the scope of the tax).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This produces an overall ratio of taxable supplies to total supplies that might be, say, 40 percent.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In the following year, unless either the tax administration or the taxpayer dissents, the same ratio of 40 percent can be used for allowing input tax without asking the taxable person to keep the same detailed records.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: I. Disallowed Input Tax Tax Law Design and Drafting (volume 1; International Monetary Fund: 1996; Victor Thuronyi, ed.)

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 56 - It is increasingly common practice for states to deny input tax credits for certain kinds of supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The main group may be described as supplies of or for luxuries, amusement, or entertainment.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The precise application of a rule such as this will involve careful definitions.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, supplies of "luxuries" to a luxury business cannot be disallowed fairly if the business is thereby prevented from recovering input tax on goods it buys in order to sell.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: By contrast, expenditure on business entertainment, such as a lavish meal for members of the staff of the taxable person, may more readily be disallowed.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The justification is that these forms of input are always personal consumption.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In effect, there is considered to be a deemed supply to the person benefiting from the expenditure.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Denial of the input credit is an administratively simple mechanism for dealing with this deemed supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: There will also always be marginal cases, such as the claim that a racehorse or a yacht bearing the name of the taxable person's products is not a luxury or that a particularly expensive item is bought for the business and not for the benefit of those who own the business.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In some states, all credit for input tax on cars is disallowed, sometimes with exceptions, such as for taxis and rental cars.147 Input tax on vans or trucks is allowed.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Many states already have rules for income tax and other purposes distinguishing between cars and vans, and they can also be used for this purpose.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: J. Capital Goods For revenue protection reasons, some states have rules that require input tax on capital goods, or certain kinds of capital goods,148 to be set off over a period of years in much the same way as the deduction of capital expenditure is controlled by capital allowances or depreciation for income tax purposes.149 These rules are exceptions to the principle that, in general, no distinction is made for VAT purposes between revenue transactions and supplies and capital transactions and supplies.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: As such, rules identifying capital goods and applying limitations on credit of input tax are a breach of the fundamental principles underlying VAT because they 147

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The EC Sixth VAT Directive, supra note 3, art. 17(6), provides that "VAT shall in no circumstances be deductible on expenditure which is not strictly business expenditure, such as that on luxuries, amusements or entertainments" and provides a procedure for agreeing on these disallowances.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: However, member states have failed to agree on a common set of rules for such deductions, and the article allows existing national disallowances to continue in force.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The disallowance on cars applies in Denmark, France, Portugal, and the United Kingdom, and with exceptions in Greece, Ireland, Italy, and Spain.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If a credit is denied for cars, it will generally be appropriate to exclude from the denial cars that are used for rental or that are held for resale.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This approach was carried into the VAT in Russia and some other states of the former Soviet Union from the previous turnover tax under which expenditure on equipment did not qualify as a deduction against the sales tax payable.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The EC Sixth VAT Directive, supra note 3, provides for adjustments for input tax credits to spread the credits on equipment over five years and on immovable property over ten years, although member states have the right to disapply the rules.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: 19–20. 149 If such rules are adopted, the law must address the same issues, including the distinction between capital and revenue items, as under the income tax.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 57 - prevent—or, rather, delay—the credit of all relevant input tax.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: As delay imposes cost, these rules create a distortion.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: K. Safeguarding the Revenue Claims for input tax credits are an inherent part of VAT, which is a tax on differences.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Any attempt to curb input tax credit is therefore wrong in principle because it changes the way VAT operates from a tax on value added to a tax on gross sales prices.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: States are entitled to protect the revenue base of the VAT against abuse of the credit procedure in order to ensure that improper claims for input tax are not made.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A major threat to the integrity of the revenue base exists where input tax exceeds output tax and a claim is made for a refund to the taxable person of the amount of the excess.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In a perfect VAT system, all such claims should be allowed within the normal time scale for paying the tax.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: However, some states have encountered widespread fraud in the operation of this practice, making safeguards necessary.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Some can be linked specifically with the payment of a refund.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The state should ensure that the rules dealing with input tax credits are clear and effective so as to prevent any doubt as to the extent of entitlement.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This should also make it easier to check claims and audit taxable persons making claims.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The rules suggested in this chapter are designed to ensure timely payment of the VAT related to a supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Under these rules, occasions would frequently arise when the VAT has been paid on a supply to the tax authorities, but payment for the supply is not received until a later time.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In the extreme cases, more common in economies in transition, some or all of the payment will not be received at all, because the customer becomes insolvent or in some other way the debt becomes bad.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Payment of VAT to the tax authorities ahead of receipt of the VAT from the customer is a normal aspect of a VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This may provide a cash-flow disadvantage to the taxable person.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In many states, this disadvantage is not particularly significant because the taxable person benefits from a much greater cash-flow advantage that arises from holding VAT collected from some customers for several weeks before having to pay it to the tax authorities.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In addition, the supplier may recover some of the economic cost of the delay in payment through an interest charge on the sums outstanding.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Where this happens, the interest charge is not subject to VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In addition, where the customer is a taxable person and receives an input credit for the VAT on the transaction, the customer could use the cash saved by the input credit to pay the supplier at least the amount of VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The parties are always free to make such an arrangement as part of the terms of their sales agreement.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If they do not make such an arrangement, then the seller is in effect extending a credit to the purchaser above and beyond the cost of the goods.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Bad debts may be seen as presenting a different problem.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It is no longer one of cash flow, but of ensuring that the tax remains a tax on value added.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If payment is not received by a supplier, then the supply may result in a loss to the supplier, with no value added.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A distinction may be drawn between the case of the very slow payer and the person who cannot pay.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A Tax Law Design and Drafting (volume 1; International Monetary Fund: 1996; Victor Thuronyi, ed.)

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 58 - solution to the problem of nonpayments, as opposed to late payments, may entail a specific allowance for bad debts.150

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This allowance will amount, in effect, to the equivalent of input tax to offset any output tax paid to the tax authorities but not collected from the customer.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If this approach is followed, a definition of "bad debt" is needed to ensure that any allowance for a bad debt does not encourage slow payment.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For this reason, it is important that the mere fact of nonpayment should not make the debt bad.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It should be shown that the debt is not collectable with reasonable effort on the part of the supplier, and that a minimum set time has elapsed.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The length of that period will depend in part on the business practice of a state and on its economy.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Inflationary factors are clearly relevant, as is the usual practice for payment of bills.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Where all bills are long delayed before being settled, the period for this provision will need to be longer.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: While it is typical to provide an allowance for bad debts, there is a counterargument.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: On the assumption that finance charges are set at a level adequate to compensate for bad debts, the total group of borrowers bears the burden of bad debts through the interest payments they make.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The cost of the consumption by defaulting customers is therefore borne by other borrowers.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: But because interest is not subject to VAT, there would be an understatement of the overall tax base if the amount of bad debts were subtracted from the base, in addition to excluding interest.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The difficulty in deciding on an appropriate policy for bad debts is that not all bad debts are covered by finance charges.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Instead, suppliers may take the risk of bad debts into account in setting prices for all.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: On this assumption, it would be appropriate to provide an allowance for bad debts.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In the case of bad debts owed by customers who are themselves taxable persons, however, a bad debt allowance would not be necessary.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If an allowance for bad debts is made, there should also be a reversal of the customer's input credit, leading to a wash.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The conclusion is that the case for a bad debt allowance is not as obvious under the VAT as it is under the income tax, and that under certain assumptions such an allowance would not be needed.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Procedure and Administration A. Need for Specific VAT Rules Legislative approaches to dealing with administrative and procedural provisions of tax laws vary markedly from state to state.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It is therefore difficult to provide any general form of provision for the procedure that must be associated with the collection of VAT by taxable persons or for the administration of VAT by the tax authorities.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In general, there are distinct advantages to combining, as far as possible, the procedure and administration of VAT with that of other taxes.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If this is done, then the matter can be dealt with in common laws dealing with taxes generally and with compatible procedures.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This is more efficient for the administration and easier for taxpayers to understand.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Combining VAT and Customs Administration on Imports The case for combining the collection of VAT on imports of goods with the collection of customs duties is particularly strong.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Questions of procedure for handling VAT on imports should as far as possible follow the procedures followed for customs duty purposes, just as this chapter has assumed that the substantive law follows customs duty law.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Similarly, there is a clear case for giving the duty of collecting VAT on imports to customs officials.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For that reason, the relevant administrative provisions should be aligned to customs laws.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The simplest form of provision is one that treats VAT on the import of goods as a customs duty for all purposes of administration of VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This would mean that customs officials can use the same powers to enforce VAT on imports as they have to deal with customs duty.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This approach will ensure that powerful provisions exist to handle VAT on imports with a minimum of legal difficulty, administrative provision, and taxpayer confusion.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: C. Handling VAT on Internal Supplies There is also a strong argument for combining the administration of VAT on internal supplies with the administration of the direct taxes.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In particular, many income tax payers with business income will also be taxable persons for VAT purposes.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Many transactions will require review for both income tax and VAT purposes, although the ways in which income tax and VAT liabilities are calculated from that common base are radically different.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Despite the differences in result, many of the problems of administration of direct taxes and VAT invite similar solutions.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, the powers of auditors carrying out field audits, or those of desk officers demanding information from taxpayers or from third parties may be aligned.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: There is an additional advantage in aligning these powers in that officers will be able to gather information for the two kinds of tax liability at the same time, thereby minimizing the demands on taxpayers.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This approach also enables a cross-check on compliance with the requirements of one tax from information gathered in checking compliance with the other.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: One of the strengths of the invoice-based form of VAT is the resulting audit trail, which can be used to check other taxes.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In the light of these general remarks, this chapter discusses only those areas of administration and procedure that are peculiar to VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It is assumed that for other matters the state will have separate legislation dealing with tax administration or that the rules in the VAT law will parallel those in other tax laws.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The VAT is an invasive tax and potentially applies to every aspect of the economy.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It is impossible to set out in one law all the rules, regulations, procedures, and working practices necessary to ensure the smooth operation of a tax that can apply to several millions of transactions a day in a state.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Not only does the VAT have this invasive, and pervasive, effect, Tax Law Design and Drafting (volume 1; International Monetary Fund: 1996; Victor Thuronyi, ed.)

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: but it must also take a clear enough form so that all those charged with settling transactions and issuing VAT invoices can do so with confidence and without delay.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The laws, rules, and guidance must be effective, and the legislation is no more than the highest level of a multilayered system of providing rules and procedures.151 E. VAT Invoices A VAT invoice is an invoice, chit, till roll print, or other document152 that is issued by a taxable person who makes a taxable supply and that records the supply and the amount of VAT payable on it.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In an invoice-based VAT system, as described in this chapter, the issue of invoices in the proper form is an essential part of the procedure for imposing and enforcing the VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The requirement that a special invoice be issued is a feature unique to VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: An invoice is a "VAT invoice" if it complies with the requirement of the VAT law.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Invoices issued for other purposes or that do not comply with these requirements do not count as VAT invoices.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: VAT laws typically condition the allowance of a credit for input tax on the existence of a VAT invoice issued during the period for which the credit is claimed.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: An invoice is also required by the tax authorities to audit the collection of VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: To allow these requirements to be met, the law should require a supplier making a taxable supply to another taxable person to provide a VAT invoice with that supply or the payment for it.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The requirement should be enforceable by some penalty or procedure.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The law could further specify that the purchaser's copy of the invoice, once created, is the property of the tax authorities, and not of the supplier or the purchaser.153 The timing rules noted previously154 are linked to the time of issue of a VAT invoice.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For that reason, together with the reasons noted in this paragraph, the supplier is usually required to issue the VAT invoice at the same time as, or soon after, the supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, the law might require the supplier to issue a VAT invoice no more than seven days after the delivery of goods or payment for those goods.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This type of short time delay ensures that an invoice in respect of a transaction, say, at the end of the last working day of a week can be legally issued at the beginning of the following week.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: 152 There is a strong case for providing in regulations for paper records to be substituted by electronic records in some cases, provided that the requirements of evidence for effective auditing are also met.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This would impose a duty on the person holding the invoice to preserve it and produce it on demand.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 61 - A VAT invoice is normally required to be identified as such (perhaps by having the words "VAT invoice" on it) and to contain a minimum of information about the supply being invoiced.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: That information would normally include155 • the name, address, and VAT number of the taxable person making the supply, • the nature of the supply made (type of supply, type of goods or services, and quantity of goods or extent of services), • the time the supply was made, • the amount of payment for the supply, • the amount of VAT, • the name, address, and VAT number of the taxable person supplied, • the date on which the invoice is issued, and • the serial number of the invoice (together with identification of the printer if the invoice was purchased privately).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A state may not need to include all this information.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, if there is only one rate of VAT, then it is redundant to state both the amount of VAT and the amount of payment for the supply.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The redundancy may, however, be considered appropriate in light of the fact that taxpayers can make computational mistakes, particularly if both exempt and taxable sales are shown on the same invoice.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The requirement to include all this information will make a VAT invoice a formal document.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This will not be appropriate for small transactions, for example, those made by a retail store, particularly where the customer is not a taxable person.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: States frequently allow special simplified invoices for small transactions or for transactions recorded in a retail store in a till or cash register.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, in these cases, it will not be required that the details of the customer be recorded unless, perhaps, the customer wishes it.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For the sake of clarity, the law should distinguish between the formal VAT invoice156 and simplified invoices.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Only the VAT invoice will entitle the purchaser to a credit for the VAT shown on the invoice, and special procedures will apply to the VAT invoice that do not apply to simplified invoices.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: While the basic distinction should be drawn in the law, matters such as acceptable forms for simplified invoices are best dealt with by regulation and guidance.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It will make for efficient administration if the tax authorities produce examples of the forms of VAT invoices acceptable to them that comply with the law.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: However, it is better that this level of detail be omitted from the main legislation.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Flexibility should be provided, for example, to allow computer-issued invoices.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: F. VAT Returns 155 See, e.g., The Value Added Tax (General) Regulations 1985, art.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: 13, reprinted in Butterworths VAT Handbook 1995, at 465.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 62 - The other essential document in administering a VAT is the required provision of information at regular intervals by all taxable persons.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This provision of information and the document on which the information is provided is commonly known in English as a "return."

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: There should be a standard form of return, so that taxable persons know precisely what is required of them and can comply more easily with the formalities of making a return, and so that the tax administration can process returns efficiently.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: All taxable persons should be required to make a return of their taxable transactions and other relevant information at predetermined and regular intervals.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The return should cover all taxable transactions made by the taxable person during the VAT period and should show how much VAT is payable to the tax authorities for that period.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The essential information on a return is therefore the following: • the total VAT collected on all taxable supplies made by the taxable person (output tax) in the VAT period, • the total VAT paid by the taxable person on supplies made to the taxable person in the VAT period and for which a credit is allowed (the allowable VAT credit or input tax deduction), • the amount of any bad debts to be set off against output tax in that VAT period, and • the amount of any excess of allowable input tax over output tax in the previous VAT period that can be carried forward (allowable excess VAT credit or input tax deduction).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The requirement that a return be made for each VAT period needs to be enforceable, with a reasonably strict time limit for submission, such as within 15 days of the last day of the VAT period to which the return relates.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A return should be required even if the taxable person has no taxable supplies for a VAT period.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This rule allows efficient operation of systems to detect and chase after persons who are delinquent in filing.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: G. Payment of VAT The law should also specify that all taxable persons must pay to the tax authorities at a specified time the net amount of VAT due for the VAT period (i.e., all VAT collected (output tax) less allowable VAT credit (deduction for input tax) and any allowable excess VAT credit carryover and VAT with respect to bad debts).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 63 - The duty to pay is usually on a self-assessment basis (i.e., the taxpayer itself determines the amount due by filling out the return).

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Each taxable person is responsible for paying the VAT due to the tax authorities in respect of any VAT period at the same time as (or, if convenient, separately but before) the return for that period is due.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Some states require advance payments of VAT, for example, three times a month, based on VAT liability for previous periods.158 The advance payments are then credited against the VAT due with the return.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: H. Assessing VAT Where a return has not been made by a taxable person (including persons not registered for VAT that should be registered or importers not covered by the import procedures) for a period for which a return should have been made, the tax authorities should be given reserve powers to impose an obligation on the taxable person to pay VAT to the tax authorities.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: For example, the tax authorities can be empowered to make a formal assessment159 of the estimated amount of VAT that a taxable person or other person is believed to owe to the tax authorities in accordance with the law.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The tax authorities should also have the power to collect any other VAT, estimated amounts of VAT, or sums equivalent to VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This can deal, for example, with an unauthorized person issuing what purports to be a VAT invoice.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The "VAT" collected by that person is due to the tax authorities, and the power to assess could provide the most convenient way of doing this.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The power to assess should also be available to deal with cases where the tax authorities have reason to believe that the returns made by a taxable person are not accurate and do not show the full amount of VAT due from that person.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The tax administration law should deal with the formalities of making assessments and procedures for challenging them.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: I. VAT Periods The payment of VAT to the tax authorities is linked to a "VAT period" as explained previously.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The length of a VAT period is a policy matter for the state.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The standard period is the calendar month; often, taxable persons with small levels of taxable turnover are allowed to use longer periods of three months or a year.160 The VAT period should be distinguished from payment periods.161 Thus, for example, a state may require enterprises of a certain size to make 158 E.g., KAZ TC art.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The process is an inherent part of the income tax in most states, and it will be efficient to apply the same procedures used for the income tax, except for those that are not relevant to VAT.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In economies with high levels of inflation, shorter periods may be appropriate.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Chapter 6, Value-Added Tax - 64 - advance payments of VAT three times a month, while the VAT period remains a calendar month.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: J. Repayment of Excess VAT Credit Where the input tax credit for any VAT period exceeds the output tax collected, there is an excess of VAT credit or of deductible input tax.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: As a direct result, the taxable person will pay no VAT to the tax authorities for that period.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: However, should the tax authorities pay the difference to the taxable person?

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: VAT is fundamentally different from direct taxes in that it involves regular situations where a taxable person is owed money from the tax authorities.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: This is an essential feature of VAT if it is truly a proportional tax based on regular VAT periods.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: The situation will arise, for example, where the taxable person buys expensive equipment or machinery costing more than the total of taxable supplies made by the taxable person during that VAT period.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: It also arises if the law makes provision for rebating tax to exporters.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Policymakers may be tempted to reduce or abolish the right for taxable persons to demand payments from the tax authorities, especially where state budgets are under pressure.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: There is an opposite temptation on political representatives to make the operation of VAT "fair" by imposing the same tight timetables on the tax authorities rebating VAT as on taxable persons paying it.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Both temptations can present major problems for the state and the tax authorities if the rules concerning VAT refunds are not carefully formulated and applied.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: A failure to allow any repayment of excess input tax undermines the fairness and economic neutrality of VAT collection.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: If applied to exporters and other similar taxable persons, it can harm the economic competitiveness of those persons and therefore of the state.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: By contrast, a regime demanding early rebates of excess VAT credit or excess deductible input tax places a tax authority at a disadvantage in dealing with evasion and fraud.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In particular, there is a danger that rebates will be given in situations where an input tax credit has been claimed for a supply but the supplier (or alleged supplier) of the supply (or alleged supply) has not paid an output tax to the tax authorities.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: There is also a danger of persons representing themselves as taxable persons when they are not, in order to claim input tax repayments when they have no intention of paying more than a nominal amount of output tax to the tax authorities.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: In the worst case, the so-called taxable person will simply disappear after receiving the credit, having made money from the tax authorities.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: There will also be cases where an expenditure that is not made for business purposes is said to be made for business purposes (e.g., on the purchase of a car or boat), so that an input tax repayment is made for input tax not paid out for business purposes.

meta.title: Tax Law Design and Drafting, Volume 1: Chapter 6: Value-Added Tax (1996)
meta.creator: Unknown

text: Balancing these two pressures on a tax authority has proved problematic in a number of states.
